newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW-Insurers seen set for shake out in Asia.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Insurers seen set for shake out in Asia.

text.p: Consolidation among Western insurers in Asia could see a shake out of firms unable to survive in an intensively competitive market with rates at record lows, a senior executive said on Monday.
"There definitely has to be consolidation," said Eric Yeo, general manager of CNA Reinsurance Co Ltd, Singapore branch.
"Those companies that haven't got the stamina or the financial resources are going to have to go back home," Yeo told Reuters in an interview.
"Asia is not an easy market. It's flooded with capital and flooded with competitors," Yeo said.

CNA Re Singapore officially opened its doors in May after its London parent -- the second largest player in the London company market by premium volume -- announced in February it had won a licence to open a branch underwriting office in Singapore.
Singapore has developed rapidly as the seat of regional reinsurance.

In January 1996, Singapore had 38 registered reinsurers, with the vast majority parented by Western companies. By May 1997, the number had expanded to almost 50 with the majority underwriting on a regional basis.

The resultant flood of capital into the region has pushed rates to rock bottom as reinsurers scramble to get a slice of a market which promises the most active growth in the world over the next decade -- 10 percent in Asia to the turn of the century compared with an average of 4 percent elsewhere.
"Reinsurers are very conservative about their estimates when they come here (to Asia) now. Most would be happy to have enough premium just to cover costs," Yeo said.
But while the concentration of players has brought pricing pressures, it has also created a real regional market in Singapore he said.
"The conventional business is being shown less and less to insurers and reinsurers outside of the region.
"Specialist lines like satellite or aviation are still shown mainly in London, but things like property, marine cargo and standard risks are more and more retained in the region," Yeo said.
